title: In the woods
hook: in the woods we return to reason and faith (Nature 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was once in a thousand years: the stars come out every night, and so we stop looking. Your line was once in a thousand years.

Reason and faith. Put those two words side by side at a dinner table and you might start an argument, with someone casting them as rivals. Emerson, in the first chapter of Nature, puts them in the same sentence, on the same path, among trees. He doesn't say the woods give you one or the other. He says you get both back. And the word he uses is return, as though both were yours once, and you wandered off.
screen: `REASON AND FAITH.` → `CAST AS RIVALS.` → `IN THE SAME SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the age you are in the woods. "In the woods, is perpetual youth." There, Emerson says, a person sheds their years the way a snake sheds its skin, and at any age is a child again. Not childish. Fresh. Second, the line itself. "In the woods, we return to reason and faith." Reason: the clear, unhurried mind that can see what's true. Faith: trust, a sense that the world holds together. Emerson doesn't make them fight; both come back when the noise drops away. Third, the promise. Among the trees, he says, he feels nothing can happen to him in life, no disgrace, no disaster, that nature can't repair, as long as he keeps his eyes. That's a big claim, and it's his, from a man who had buried his young wife. He isn't saying nothing will hurt. He's saying the woods are a place where repair begins. Fourth, where the paragraph goes next. Standing on bare ground, he writes, all mean egotism vanishes. "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all." That eye-ball had a day of its own, back on day one thousand twenty-two. The self gets small, and the seeing gets large: among trees, you stop being the center of the picture. Far from any forest, that might be a single tree on a city street, a park at lunch, a row of bushes by a bus stop.
screen: `IN THE WOODS, IS PERPETUAL YOUTH.` · `REASON AND FAITH COME BACK.` · `NOTHING NATURE CANNOT REPAIR.` · `A TRANSPARENT EYE-BALL.` · then, large: `IN THE WOODS, WE RETURN TO REASON AND FAITH.`

segments.voice: If you can, go outside and walk slowly toward the nearest tree; if you can't, bring to mind the last time you stood among trees, the smell, the light through leaves, the sound underfoot. Either way, let your mind get quiet enough to notice two things, something clear and something steady, without needing to name them reason and faith.
In the woods. Emerson's place of perpetual youth, where, he says, we return to reason and faith, and the self becomes a transparent eye. Today's word.
Your line: in the woods. Emerson's word is return, as if you'd been there before. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson's Nature often take walks among trees as a quiet practice of their own, sometimes carrying this passage with them, to let reason and trust settle at the same time.

notes: Three quotations from Nature, ch. 1; confirm wording and punctuation (including 'eye-ball' with the hyphen) against the first edition.
Writer cut a line about friends teasing Emerson over the transparent eyeball (the Cranch caricature); 'some readers laugh at that eyeball' remains and could also be cut.
'A man who had buried his young wife' refers back to day 1186.
The closing line ('the woods can be smaller than we think') replaces a general claim about Concord; fine to cut.
The hook says reason and faith are often framed as rivals ('people say'); this is a light framing of everyday talk, not a claim about any tradition; soften if needed.
